      {"@context":"http://schema.org","@graph":[{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Public Service Commission Te Kawa Mataaho","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/te-kawa-mataaho"},"datePublished":"2026-07-30T22:01:28.901Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/te-kawa-mataaho_we-have-released-the-findings-of-an-independent-activity-7488715416610070528-3CF3","text":"We have released the findings of an independent review into social media messages posted during collective bargaining and the lead-up to the public sector ‘day of action’ in October 2025.

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche initiated the review to provide assurance about the decision-making processes that were followed and to identify any lessons for the future.

The review found there is scope for improvement.

It found that the Commission was operating in a challenging environment, balancing its responsibilities as the employer in education sector bargaining with its broader leadership role across the Public Service. In that context, the review found the Commissioner was entitled to communicate publicly about bargaining progress and the potential disruption arising from strike action.

The review found:

• the messaging was not sufficiently adapted to the social media environment, which increased the risk of the content not being seen as politically neutral.

•without the context provided in media statements and interviews, recipients of the social media messages might not have understood the Commissioner was required to advocate for his position as the employer in bargaining.

• the Commission’s media statements, and the tiles (social media posts), did not breach political neutrality.

• the Commission’s integrity analysis was robust and appropriately identified risks, but the Commission moved too quickly and did not spend enough time working through the implications of using paid social media advertising.

• there was no direction from Ministers to undertake the social media campaign.

“I accept the review’s findings and recommendations,” Sir Brian said.

“The review does not find we were directed by Ministers. It does not find that we breached political neutrality. But it did find we should have handled this more carefully. I accept that.

“We did the right thing in seeking integrity advice. Where we fell short was not giving ourselves enough time to fully work through that advice before paid social media posts were published.

“The lesson for us is clear. In a high-risk situation, particularly one involving our own conduct, we need to be more deliberate in our steps, fully consider the advice, and make sure our decision-making is as robust as it should be.”

The review makes a number of recommendations to strengthen future decision-making, including allowing more time for integrity analysis, considering external peer review of advice in high-risk situations, and strengthening sign-off arrangements for contentious decisions.

Read the media statement and review report here:

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We have released the findings of an independent review into social media messages posted during collective bargaining and the lead-up to the public sector ‘day of action’ in October 2025.

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche initiated the review to provide assurance about the decision-making processes that were followed and to identify any lessons for the future.

The review found there is scope for improvement.

It found that the Commission was operating in a challenging environment, balancing its responsibilities as the employer in education sector bargaining with its broader leadership role across the Public Service. In that context, the review found the Commissioner was entitled to communicate publicly about bargaining progress and the potential disruption arising from strike action.

The review found:

• the messaging was not sufficiently adapted to the social media environment, which increased the risk of the content not being seen as politically neutral.

•without the context provided in media statements and interviews, recipients of the social media messages might not have understood the Commissioner was required to advocate for his position as the employer in bargaining.

• the Commission’s media statements, and the tiles (social media posts), did not breach political neutrality.

• the Commission’s integrity analysis was robust and appropriately identified risks, but the Commission moved too quickly and did not spend enough time working through the implications of using paid social media advertising.

• there was no direction from Ministers to undertake the social media campaign.

“I accept the review’s findings and recommendations,” Sir Brian said.

“The review does not find we were directed by Ministers. It does not find that we breached political neutrality. But it did find we should have handled this more carefully. I accept that.

“We did the right thing in seeking integrity advice. Where we fell short was not giving ourselves enough time to fully work through that advice before paid social media posts were published.

“The lesson for us is clear. In a high-risk situation, particularly one involving our own conduct, we need to be more deliberate in our steps, fully consider the advice, and make sure our decision-making is as robust as it should be.”

The review makes a number of recommendations to strengthen future decision-making, including allowing more time for integrity analysis, considering external peer review of advice in high-risk situations, and strengthening sign-off arrangements for contentious decisions.

Read the media statement and review report here:

  <div class="attributed-text-segment-list__container relative mt-1 mb-1.5 babybear:mt-0 babybear:mb-0.5">
    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Today we join many across New Zealand in mourning the loss of Dame Helene Quilter DNZM QSO.

Dame Helene dedicated 45 years to public service, serving with distinction as Secretary of Defence, Deputy Commissioner of the State Services Commission, and Deputy Public Service Commissioner at Public Service Commission Te Kawa Mataaho. Her career was defined by an unwavering commitment to strengthening the institutions that serve New Zealanders and to developing the people who lead them.

She was a champion of public service excellence, diversity, and a trusted leader whose influence can be seen across generations of public servants. Her contributions helped shape a stronger, more capable and more representative Public Service.

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche said:

"Dame Helene was an outstanding public servant whose legacy will be felt across New Zealand for generations to come. She combined intellectual rigour with humanity, integrity with courage, and a deep understanding of what it means to serve the public good."

Our thoughts are with her husband Geoff, her family, friends, former colleagues, and the many people whose lives and careers were enriched by her leadership, mentorship and friendship.

Ngā mihi nui, Dame Helene. Thank you for your remarkable service to New Zealand. Your legacy will endure.</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Creating accessible public services is a shared responsibility across government.

The Government Digital Delivery Agency is consulting on a new Digital Accessibility Standard that will help ensure accessibility is considered across all digital technology, not just websites.

While the current Web Accessibility Standard applies only to websites and web apps, the proposed standard is expected to apply across all information and communication technology. This includes documents, software and hardware.

The new standard would support a more consistent approach to accessibility across government and help make digital information and services more accessible for all New Zealanders.

Consultation on the draft standard is now open and closes at 5pm on Friday 7 August. Information is available in a range of alternate formats.

"The receipt of this scholarship is both a privilege, and an encouragement from my hoa mahi and community to begin the next chapter of my journey through studying a Bachelor of Finance and Business Analytics.
